frontpage.description: Mississippi, a state with the largest share of Black residents in the country, has elected its first Black U.S. senator in nearly 150 years. Why it matters: For generations, Black Mississippians left the state to escape Jim Crow and pursue economic and political opportunities elsewhere.

sources.name: The Guardian US
sources.title: Mississippi makes history with Democrat Scott Colom’s Senate win - The Latest
sources.description: Mississippi has elected the Democrat Scott Colom in a historic race in the traditionally deep-red state, making him its first Black senator since shortly after the US civil war. The closely contested race was called more than a week after the US midterms, with Colom running against the Republican incumbent, Cindy Hyde-Smith.

sources.name: Slate
sources.title: Lessons on Scott Colom’s Win From Mississippi’s First Black Senator
sources.description: In January 1870, the Mississippi Legislature elected Hiram R. Revels to take the seat vacated when Albert Gallatin Brown resigned from the Senate.

sources.name: The New York Times
sources.title: In Mississippi, Scott Colom Supporters Celebrate Historic Senate Win
sources.description: At Tougaloo College, supporters danced and wept over Scott Colom’s victory. He will be Mississippi’s first Black U.S. senator since the Reconstruction era.

sources.name: NBC News Politics
sources.title: Mississippi Elects First Black Senator in More Than 140 Years
sources.description: Democrat Scott Colom defeated incumbent Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi’s race for U.S. Senate, making Colom the state’s first Black senator elected since Reconstruction and its first Democratic senator in nearly 45 years. NBC’s Garrett Haake reports for TODAY.

sources.name: The Atlantic
sources.title: Scott Colom Is Mississippi’s First Black Senator in 150 Years
sources.description: This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter. Sign up for it here. One fall afternoon in Liberty, Mississippi, in 1961, a white Democratic former congressman and state legislator named E. H. Hurst shot Herbert Lee in the head. Hurst was angry that Lee, who was Black, had been trying to register other Black Mississippians to vote.

sources.name: Fast Company
sources.title: Democrat Scott Colom wins in Mississippi to become the state’s first Black senator since Reconstruction
sources.description: Democratic nominee Scott Colom defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith on Wednesday in Mississippi’s closely contested U.S. Senate race after a prolonged ballot counting process, giving the state its first Black U.S. senator since post-Civil War Reconstruction.

sources.title: Democrat Scott Colom wins Mississippi Senate race
sources.description: Scott Colom has won the U.S. Senate race in Mississippi. After a very close race, he's the first Black man to represent the state in the Senate in nearly 150 years.

sources.name: NBC News Politics
sources.title: Democrat Scott Colom wins Mississippi Senate seat, breaking GOP’s grip on the state
sources.description: Colom pulled off an upset over Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, becoming the first Democrat elected to the Senate in Mississippi since 1982.

sources.name: Politico
sources.title: Mississippi elects Democrat Scott Colom to Senate in massive upset
sources.description: Mississippi voted blue, in a shock win for Democrats. Democrat Scott Colom ousted Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in a state that went for President Donald Trump by 23 points in 2024. He will be the first Black senator elected in Mississippi since the Reconstruction era — and the first Democrat from the state headed to the Senate in 44 years.

sources.title: How Scott Colom defied the odds to go from DA to Mississippi's Democratic U.S. senator

headlines.name: American Cancer Society revises guidelines, urges routine PSA screening for prostate cancer
headlines.headline: American Cancer Society revises guidelines, urges routine PSA screening for prostate cancer
headlines.description: In a major change to screening guidelines, the American Cancer Society recommended on Thursday that American men between ages 50 and 69 at an average risk of prostate cancer should test their prostate-specific antigen (PSA) blood levels every two years. The prior guidelines, released in 2010, left testing for average-risk men to their discretion, after assessing cancer risk with a physician.
